title: Out of the depths (Psalm 129 [130])
hookLine: the psalm prayed for the dead

cards: Some nights you're not on the road anymore. You're at the bottom of something. A diagnosis.
A funeral. A mistake you can't take back. A phone call at three in the morning.
Words run out, and you can't manage anything polished or brave. Down there, people have reached for the same short psalm for well over two thousand years. Monks sang it at evening prayer.
Families say it at gravesides. A well-known writer's letter from prison was published under its first two Latin words.

teach.b: It opens at the lowest point. In the Douay-Rheims: "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." In Latin, De profundis clamavi ad te, Domine.
First, the depths. In the Bible the deep waters are chaos and drowning, the place where your feet can't touch. The psalmist is in over his head, and he says so.

The prayer doesn't wait until he's feeling better; it starts from the bottom. Second, the turn. Next he speaks of sin, disarmingly honest: "If thou, O Lord, wilt mark iniquities: Lord, who shall stand it."

teach.h: IF YOU KEPT A LEDGER, WHO COULD STAND?
teach.b: If God kept a ledger, nobody would last. Then the hinge: with God there is forgiveness. That's why this is one of the seven penitential psalms.

teach.h: THE CHURCH'S PSALM FOR THE DEAD.
teach.b: The psalm doesn't end with rescue. It ends with hope that keeps going around the clock: "My soul hath hoped in the Lord. From the morning watch even until night, let Israel hope in the Lord."
The Hebrew pictures a watchman on the wall, waiting for dawn. Anyone who has sat up with someone sick knows that watch, waiting for the window to go gray. Fourth, the dead.

teach.h: OUT OF THE DEPTHS I HAVE CRIED TO THEE.
teach.b: Because it cries from the depths and hopes for mercy, the Church took this psalm as its prayer for those who have died.
It's sung in the Office of the Dead, and for centuries Catholics have prayed the De profundis for the souls of the faithful departed, often at graves, often in the evening.
Catholics believe the prayers of the living can help the dead on their way to God.

how: Catholics pray the De profundis for the dead, in the Office of the Dead, at funerals and gravesides, and especially in November; it is also prayed at Night Prayer on Wednesdays in the Liturgy of the Hours.

a Christmas carol for midnight Mass
the deep things of God, a hymn of mystery

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: if God kept one, who could stand?

s: the psalm waits until the psalmist feels better
it starts at the bottom: "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord."
it is one of the seven penitential psalms
it's honest about sin and turns on forgiveness.
the psalm ends with a rescue
it ends with waiting and hope, like a watchman waiting for dawn.

games.q: you're in the depths, and you think: if God kept a record of every wrong, nobody could stand. what does the psalm say next?
o: so try harder to be perfect.
games.why: the hinge of the psalm: with God there is forgiveness, and so the psalmist waits and hopes.

practice: Let one person who has died come to mind: a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to. Remember one ordinary thing about them, the way they laughed, what they always cooked.
If you pray, pray the psalm's first line for them, out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord; if you don't, keep a quiet minute in their memory.

wordCard.voice: De profundis. Latin for out of the depths: the first words of the psalm the Church prays for the dead. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: out of the depths, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate and its name in the Church.

carryVoice: Your line: my soul hath hoped. Even from the depths, the watchman waits for morning. Until tomorrow.
